Now, regarding the second part of your question, a step function f / [a, b] -> \mathbb{R} is Riemann Integrable. This statement is true, and I can provide a proof.

Let f be a step function on the interval [a, b]. Then, f can be written as a finite linear combination of indicator functions of intervals:

f(x) = ∑_{i=1}^n c_i \chi_{I_i}(x)

where I_i are disjoint intervals, c_i are constants, and n is a positive integer.

To prove that f is Riemann Integrable, we need to show that the upper and lower Riemann sums converge to the same value as the partition size approaches 0.

Let P be a partition of [a, b] into n subintervals, and let M_i and m_i be the supremum and infimum of f on I_i, respectively. Then, the upper Riemann sum is:

U(P) = ∑_{i=1}^n M_i \Delta x_i

where \Delta x_i is the length of the subinterval I_i.

Similarly, the lower Riemann sum is:

L(P) = ∑_{i=1}^n m_i \Delta x_i

Since f is a step function, the supremum and infimum of f on each interval I_i are constants, say M_i and m_i, respectively. Therefore, the upper and lower Riemann sums can be rewritten as:

U(P) = ∑_{i=1}^n M_i \Delta x_i = ∑_{i=1}^n c_i M_i \Delta x_i

L(P) = ∑_{i=1}^n m_i \Delta x_i = ∑_{i=1}^n c_i m_i \Delta x_i

Since the intervals I_i are disjoint, the sum of the lengths of the subintervals is equal to the length of the interval [a, b], i.e., ∑_{i=1}^n \Delta x_i = b-a.

Now, we can rewrite the upper and lower Riemann sums as:

U(P) = ∑_{i=1}^n c_i M_i (b-a)

L(P) = ∑_{i=1}^n c_i m_i (b-a)

As the partition size approaches 0, the upper and lower Riemann sums converge to the same value, which is equal to the integral of f over the interval [a, b].

Therefore, we have shown that the step function f is Riemann Integrable.

Note that this proof assumes that the step function f is defined on a finite interval [a, b]. If the interval is infinite, the proof requires additional assumptions or modifications.
